title: DistillKac: Few-Step Image Generation via Damped Wave Equations
claim: Our generator produces diverse, high-fidelity, uncurated samples across datasets, which shows its sample quality without any method diagram.
layout: 2 panels side by side, each a dense grid of samples with thick black borders (left 7x10 CIFAR-10, right 4x5 CelebA-64 faces)
description: The figure is a pure sample gallery in two framed panels. The left panel shows a 7-row by 10-column grid of small CIFAR-10 images. Each column matches one class, in order: airplane, car, bird, cat, deer, dog, frog, horse, ship, truck. The right panel shows a 4-row by 5-column grid of larger CelebA-64 face images with varied gender, age, hair color, pose and expression. Thin black gridlines separate the tiles, and a thick black border frames each panel. There are no arrows, labels, axes or text inside the image. The eye goes first to the colorful faces on the right, then scans the CIFAR grid. The figure relies on visual realism and diversity to show sample quality.
caption: Uncurated CIFAR-10 (left) and CelebA-64 (right) samples generated by Guided Kac Flow (midpoint integrator, 100 steps, guidance $w = 3$ for CIFAR-10 and $w = 0$ for CelebA-64).
abstract: We present DistillKac, a fast image generator that uses the damped wave equation and its stochastic Kac representation to move probability mass at finite speed. In contrast to diffusion models whose reverse time velocities can become stiff and implicitly allow unbounded propagation speed, Kac dynamics enforce finite speed transport and yield globally bounded kinetic energy. Building on this structure, we introduce classifier-free guidance in velocity space that preserves square integrability under mild conditions. We then propose endpoint only distillation that trains a student to match a frozen teacher over long intervals. We prove a stability result that promotes supervision at the endpoints to closeness along the entire path. Experiments demonstrate DistillKac delivers high quality samples with very few function evaluations while retaining the numerical stability benefits of finite speed probability flows.
